Asymptotic Variance-Covariance Matrices of Item Parameter Estimates

Source: R/covirt.R
covirt.Rd

This function computes the analytical asymptotic variance-covariance matrices of item parameter estimates for dichotomous and polytomous IRT models without examinee response data. For each item, the matrix is the inverse of the expected (Fisher) information of the item parameters, which is integrated over an assumed ability distribution and multiplied by the calibration sample size (Thissen & Wainer, 1982; Li & Lissitz, 2004). The square roots of the diagonal elements are the asymptotic standard errors of the maximum likelihood estimates.

Usage

covirt(
  x,
  D = 1,
  nstd = 1000,
  pcm.loc = NULL,
  norm.prior = c(0, 1),
  nquad = 41,
  weights = NULL
)

Arguments

x

A data frame containing item metadata (item IDs, numbers of score categories, IRT models, and item parameters). The item parameters are treated as the true values at which the information is evaluated; for 1PLM items and for PCM items specified in pcm.loc, the slope in x is held fixed. See est_irt() or simdat() for the format of the item metadata, which can be created with shape_df().

D

A scaling constant used in IRT models to make the logistic function closely approximate the normal ogive function. A value of 1.702 is commonly used for this purpose. Default is 1.

nstd

An integer, or a vector of integers with one value per item in x, giving the number of examinees used to calibrate the items. The information of each item is multiplied by its sample size, so the standard errors are proportional to 1 / sqrt(nstd). Default is 1000. See Details.

pcm.loc

A vector of integers giving the positions (rows of x) of GPCM items that were calibrated with the partial credit model (PCM). For these items, the slope is held at the value in x and the variance-covariance matrices are computed only for the threshold parameters. Positions of items that are not GPCM items are ignored. Default is NULL. See Details.

norm.prior

A numeric vector of length two specifying the mean and standard deviation of the normal ability distribution over which the information is integrated. Used to generate the Gaussian quadrature points and weights when weights = NULL. Default is c(0, 1).

nquad

An integer specifying the number of Gaussian quadrature points generated from the normal distribution given in norm.prior. Used only when weights = NULL. Default is 41.

weights

An optional two-column data frame or matrix of quadrature points (first column) and weights (second column) that defines the ability distribution. The weights should sum to 1, because they are not normalized. If weights is supplied, norm.prior and nquad are ignored. Such a data frame can be created with gen.weight(). Default is NULL.

Value

A named list with the following two components:

  • cov: A named list of variance-covariance matrices, one per item. Each matrix contains only the estimated parameters of the item, and its row and column names are the parameter columns of x: par.2 (difficulty) for the 1PLM; par.1 and par.2 (slope and difficulty) for the 2PLM; par.1 to par.3 (slope, difficulty, and guessing) for the 3PLM; par.1 to par.K (slope and K - 1 thresholds) for GRM and GPCM items with K score categories; and par.2 to par.K (thresholds only) for PCM items specified in pcm.loc. Covariances between parameters of different items are not computed. If the information matrix of an item is singular, a warning is issued and the matrix is filled with NA.

  • se: A named list of vectors containing the asymptotic standard errors (ASEs) of the item parameter estimates, computed as the square roots of the diagonal elements of each corresponding variance-covariance matrix in cov.

The names of the list elements in both cov and se correspond to the item identifiers (e.g., item names or labels) as given in the first column of the input x.

Details

For each item, the asymptotic variance-covariance matrix is the inverse of the expected (Fisher) information matrix of the item parameters, which is integrated over the ability distribution with quadrature and multiplied by the sample size (Thissen & Wainer, 1982; Li & Lissitz, 2004). For an item with \(K\) score categories, the element of the information matrix for a pair of item parameters \(\xi_s\) and \(\xi_t\) is

$$I(\xi_s, \xi_t) = N \sum_{q=1}^{Q} A(X_q) \sum_{k=1}^{K} \frac{1}{P_k(X_q)} \frac{\partial P_k(X_q)}{\partial \xi_s} \frac{\partial P_k(X_q)}{\partial \xi_t},$$

where \(N\) is the sample size (nstd), \(X_q\) and \(A(X_q)\) are the \(Q\) quadrature points and weights that represent the ability distribution (norm.prior and nquad, or weights), and \(P_k(X_q)\) is the probability of a response in category \(k\) at \(X_q\). This is the information of a categorical (multinomial) response. For a dichotomous item, it reduces to the familiar form in which each term is divided by \(P(X_q) [1 - P(X_q)]\) (Li & Lissitz, 2004, Equation A4).

For polytomous items, the information above differs from Equation A8 of Li and Lissitz (2004). Their Equation A6 writes the likelihood of a response (and Equation A7 its logarithm) as \(\prod_{k} P_k^{u_k} (1 - P_k)^{1 - u_k}\), where \(u_k\) is 1 for the observed category and 0 otherwise. The \(K\) category indicators are thus treated as independent Bernoulli variables, and Equation A8 accordingly divides each term by \(P_k (1 - P_k)\) instead of \(P_k\). However, the indicators of one response sum to 1, so the response follows a multinomial distribution with likelihood \(\prod_{k} P_k^{u_k}\), whose information divides each term by \(P_k\) only. Because \(1 - P_k < 1\), Equation A8 overstates the information and understates the standard errors. For example, for an item with two categories, Equation A8 gives exactly twice the information of their Equation A4 for dichotomous items. This function uses the multinomial information.

The multinomial information was checked by a simulation that matches the setting of this function: abilities drawn from N(0, 1) and treated as known, maximum likelihood estimation, a sample size of 1,000, and 1,000 replications for GRM and GPCM items with three to five categories. The standard errors from the multinomial information agreed with the standard deviations of the estimates across replications (ratios of 0.96 to 1.08), whereas those from Equation A8 were about 10 to 23 percent smaller (ratios of 0.77 to 0.90). For a dichotomous (2PLM) item, the two forms give the same results.

The matrices are derived under the assumptions that the IRT model fits the data, that the item parameters are estimated by maximum likelihood, and that the ability distribution is known (Li & Lissitz, 2004). Because the abilities are treated as known, the uncertainty in the abilities is ignored, and prior distributions on the item parameters are not taken into account. The resulting standard errors are therefore generally considered lower bounds of the standard errors of an actual calibration (Thissen & Wainer, 1982). They may serve as approximations for evaluating the precision of item parameter estimates when empirical standard errors are not reported.

If the item parameters provided in the x argument were calibrated using different sample sizes, a corresponding vector of sample sizes must be specified via the nstd argument. For example, suppose you wish to compute the variance-covariance matrices of five 3PLM items that were calibrated using 500, 600, 1,000, 2,000, and 700 examinees, respectively. In this case, set nstd = c(500, 600, 1000, 2000, 700).

Since the item metadata allows only "GPCM" to denote both the partial credit model (PCM) and the generalized partial credit model (GPCM), PCM items must be explicitly identified using the pcm.loc argument. For these items, the slope is not treated as an estimated parameter: it is held at the value in x, and only the threshold parameters enter the information matrix. For instance, if the last two of five polytomous items were calibrated using the PCM, specify pcm.loc = c(4, 5). A GRM or GPCM item with two score categories is treated as a 2PLM item, and a PCM item with two score categories as a 1PLM item with a fixed slope.

References

Li, Y. H., & Lissitz, R. W. (2004). Applications of the analytically derived asymptotic standard errors of item response theory item parameter estimates. Journal of Educational Measurement, 41(2), 85-117. doi:10.1111/j.1745-3984.2004.tb01109.x .

Thissen, D., & Wainer, H. (1982). Some standard errors in item response theory. Psychometrika, 47(4), 397-412. doi:10.1007/BF02293705 .

See also

est_irt(), simdat(), shape_df(), gen.weight()

Examples

# Example using a "-prm.txt" file exported from flexMIRT
flex_prm <- system.file("extdata", "flexmirt_sample-prm.txt", package = "irtQ")

# Select the first two dichotomous items and the last polytomous item
x <- bring.flexmirt(file = flex_prm, "par")$Group1$full_df[c(1:2, 55), ]

# Compute the variance-covariance matrices assuming a sample size of 2,000
covirt(x, D = 1, nstd = 2000, norm.prior = c(0, 1), nquad = 41)
